abstract: Deep multitask networks, in which one neural network produces multiple predictive outputs, can offer better speed and performance than their single-task counterparts but are challenging to train properly. We present a gradient normalization (GradNorm) algorithm that automatically balances training in deep multitask models by dynamically tuning gradient magnitudes. We show that for various network architectures, for both regression and classification tasks, and on both synthetic and real datasets, GradNorm improves accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple tasks when compared to single-task networks, static baselines, and other adaptive multitask loss balancing techniques. GradNorm also matches or surpasses the performance of exhaustive grid search methods, despite only involving a single asymmetry hyperparameter α\alpha. Thus, what was once a tedious search process that incurred exponentially more compute for each task added can now be accomplished within a few training runs, irrespective of the number of tasks. Ultimately, we will demonstrate that gradient manipulation affords us great control over the training dynamics of multitask networks and may be one of the keys to unlocking the potential of multitask learning.

bibliographic.title: GradNorm: Gradient Normalization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in Deep Multitask Networks
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2018)

content.problem: Training deep multitask networks is hard because task imbalances cause gradient magnitude imbalances that let dominant tasks overwhelm shared feature learning.
content.proposed_solution: The authors propose GradNorm to dynamically balance gradient magnitudes across tasks by adjusting multitask loss weights according to relative training rates.
dataset_testbed: synthetic toy multitask regression system (2-task and 10-task)
NYUv2+seg (NYUv2 with depth, surface normals, and 13-class segmentation labels)
NYUv2+kpts (augmented NYUv2 with depth, surface normals, and human-annotated room keypoints, ~90,000 images)

metrics.name: Depth
metrics.condition: Test error on NYUv2+seg with the VGG16 SegNet using GradNorm alpha=1.5

metrics.condition: Test error on NYUv2+seg with the VGG16 SegNet using GradNorm alpha=1.5

metrics.condition: Test error on NYUv2+seg with the VGG16 SegNet using GradNorm alpha=1.5

content.claim: GradNorm improves multitask accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple vision tasks while matching or exceeding the performance of exhaustive grid search.
author_stated_limitations: Tasks that become stuck during training pose an obstacle because GradNorm continually increases their loss weights.
Keypoint prediction and failure rate gains on MTFL likely fall within error bars and may not represent statistically significant improvements.

evidence.problem_quote: task imbalances impede proper training because they manifest as imbalances between backpropagated gradients. A task that is too dominant during training, for example, will necessarily express that dominance by inducing gradients which have relatively large magnitudes.
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: We present a gradient normalization (GradNorm) algorithm that automatically balances training in deep multitask models by dynamically tuning gradient magnitudes.
evidence.claim_quote: We show that for various network architectures, for both regression and classification tasks, and on both synthetic and real datasets, GradNorm improves accuracy and reduces overfitting across multiple tasks when compared to single-task networks, static baselines, and other adaptive multitask loss balancing techniques.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: Such tasks which become “stuck” during training pose a problem for GradNorm, as the GradNorm algorithm would tend to continuously increase the loss weights for these tasks.

It should be noted that the keypoint prediction and failure rate improvements are likely within error bars; a 1% absolute improvement in keypoint error represents a very fine sub-pixel improvement, and thus may not represent a statistically significant gain.
